**The CLI documents itself, and that is the authoritative reference.** Every
command carries a description, runnable examples and the endpoint it calls, so
the fastest way to learn it is to ask it:

```bash
keystonectl help              # every command, grouped
keystonectl help restart      # one command, with examples
keystonectl restart --help    # the same
```

`keystonectl help <command>` prints, among other things, the line
`Calls POST /v1/components/{name}:restart.` — the mapping from CLI to API is
in the tool, not only on this page.

Shell completion comes with it:

```bash
source <(keystonectl completion bash)   # or zsh, fish, powershell
```

### The commands

**Plan**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `apply <plan.toml>` | Upload and apply a deployment plan |
| `apply-dry <plan.toml>` | Apply a plan in dry-run mode and show the reconcile |
| `graph` | Show the dependency graph and a valid start order |
| `reconcile` | Repair the plan in effect |
| `status` | Show the applied plan, its status and its components |
| `stop-plan` | Stop every component in the plan |

**Components**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `components` | List components with state, PID and last health result |
| `restart <component>` | Restart one component, cascading to its dependents |
| `restart-dry <component>` | Show which components a restart would stop and start |
| `stop <component>` | Stop one component |

**Recipes**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `delete-recipe <name> <version>` | Remove a recipe from the agent's store |
| `recipes` | List the recipes stored in the agent |
| `upload-recipe <recipe.toml>` | Add a recipe to the agent's store |

**Agent**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `health` | Check that the agent is alive, and for how long |
| `version` | Show this client's version and commit |

**Local tools**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `manifest` | Create, sign and check dataset manifests |
| `sha256 <file>` | Compute the SHA-256 of a local file |
| `sign <file>` | Sign a file, producing a detached <file>.sig |
| `verify <file>` | Verify a detached signature the way the agent will |

### Global flags

These apply to every command.

| Flag | What it is | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--addr` | Agent base URL, resolved on the SSH host when --ssh is used (or KEYSTONE_ADDR) | `http://127.0.0.1:8080` |
| `--ssh` | Reach the agent through SSH: [user@]host[:port] (or KEYSTONE_SSH) | (none) |
| `--token` | Bearer token for the agent API (or KEYSTONE_API_TOKEN) | (none) |

A flag always wins over its environment variable, which wins over the default.

`--addr` is worth exporting when the agent does not use the default port:

```bash
export KEYSTONE_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:9180
keystonectl components
```

`restart` takes `--wait pid|health` and `--timeout`, so a script can block
until the component is actually serving:

```bash
keystonectl restart api --wait health --timeout 120s
```

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | The request succeeded |
| `1` | The agent or the network reported a failure |
| `2` | The command was used wrongly — bad arguments, bad `--ssh` destination |

Note `stop-plan` (everything) versus `stop <component>` (one thing) — they
are different commands, and the plural mistake is an outage.

Every command prints the agent's own response. A dry run reports the order it
would use, not a bare `OK`:

```console
$ keystonectl restart-dry api
{
  "startOrder": [
    "api"
  ],
  "stopOrder": null
}
```

### Reaching an agent bound to loopback

The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` by default, and binding anything else
[requires a token](../../security/api-auth/). On a real device that means its API
is only reachable from the device itself.

`--ssh` carries the request there, so there is no `ssh -L` to keep alive in
another terminal and no port to expose:

```bash
keystonectl --ssh ops@edge-001 components
keystonectl --ssh ops@edge-001:52022 --addr http://127.0.0.1:9180 restart-dry api
```

**`--addr` is resolved on the far side.** The default `http://127.0.0.1:8080` is
therefore the *agent's* loopback — exactly the interface it is bound to. Both
variables can be exported together for a device you work on often:

```bash
export KEYSTONE_SSH=ops@edge-001:52022
export KEYSTONE_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:9180
keystonectl status
```

What it does under the hood is run your own `ssh` client with `-W`, which splices
its stdio to a host and port on the far side. That is deliberate: it inherits
your `~/.ssh/config` — `Host` aliases, `IdentityFile`, `ProxyJump` through a
bastion, the agent, certificates and `known_hosts` — and the host key is verified
by `ssh` under your own rules. Keystone adds no cryptography of its own here.

The consequences are worth knowing:

- It needs the `ssh` binary on **your** machine (the device only needs `sshd`).
- The device's `sshd` must allow `AllowTcpForwarding`, which is the default but
  is sometimes turned off on a hardened image. If it is off, `-W` fails.
- SSH errors — unknown host, rejected key — reach you verbatim on stderr rather
  than as an opaque connection failure.
- `--ssh` is Unix-only. On Windows the rest of the CLI works; forward the port
  with `ssh -L` and point `--addr` at it.
